Two distinct circles meet in at most 2 points, so each of the $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ pairs contributes at most 2 intersection points.

Counting pairs of circles gives an upper bound of $6 \times 2 = 12$ on the number of distinct points. A point lying on three or more circles is counted by several pairs, so it uses up more of this budget and can only lower the total.

The bound is achieved. Take four circles with centers and radii in general position, so that each pair meets in two points and no point lies on three circles. Then all 12 intersection points are distinct.

ANSWER: 12
